introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION (GCE) BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0755 Geology 1, JUNE 2021, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, 1 hour 30 minutes. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the question booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0755 Geology - 1'; fill in the information required on the answer sheet using your HB pencil (Candidate Number, Name, Centre Number and Name); take care not to crease or fold the answer sheet or make marks on it other than those asked for. Answer ALL the 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide on which answer is correct, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question; if you change your mind, erase the first mark carefully, then mark your new answer. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet, using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet; do not attempt to leave the examination hall with it.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following planets is the largest in the Solar System in terms of mass and radius?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jupiter is the largest planet of the Solar System: its mass is about 318 times that of the Earth (about $1.9 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{kg}$) and its mean radius is about 11 times the Earth's radius (about 70 000 km). Saturn comes second (mass about 95 Earth masses). The Earth and Mars are small rocky (terrestrial) planets.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which reason below explains why Venus has a higher surface temperature than Mercury?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Venus has a very dense atmosphere made of about 96 % carbon dioxide. This causes a very strong greenhouse effect: the heat radiated by the surface is trapped, so the surface temperature stays near 460 to 470 $^\circ$C everywhere, day and night, even though Venus is farther from the Sun than Mercury. Option B is false (Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun). Options A and C describe why Mercury loses its heat, but the question asks why Venus is hotter, and the cause is the greenhouse gases of its atmosphere.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Mercury is smaller than Venus so its surface cools quickly.
Venus lies closer to the Sun than Mercury.
Mercury's atmosphere is thin so retains little heat.
Venus has a higher level of greenhouse gases than Mercury.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 1) which shows the upper 600 km of the Earth and answer questions 3 and 4.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

The layer labelled X is called?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 1 the brace Y covers the part from the surface down to about 70 km: this is the **lithosphere**, the rigid outer shell made of the crust (A, down to 35 km) and the uppermost mantle (B). The brace X lies just below it, between about 70 km and 200 km: this is the weak, partly molten and plastic layer of the upper mantle called the **asthenosphere** (the low velocity zone for seismic waves), on which the plates move. The crust and the lithosphere are above this level, and the mantle as a whole is far thicker than layer X.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The discontinuity that exists at a depth of 35 km is: (use Figure 1, shown with question 3)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 1 the line at 35 km separates the continental crust (A) from the mantle (B). This crust-mantle boundary is the **Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho)**, found at about 35 km under the continents (5 to 10 km under the oceans). The Conrad discontinuity separates the upper from the lower continental crust, the Lehmann discontinuity lies at about 5 150 km (inner core-outer core boundary), and the Gutenberg discontinuity lies at about 2 900 km (mantle-core boundary).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 2) shows paths of earthquake waves through the Earth. Use the diagram to answer questions 5 and 6.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

What does the letter X represent?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The letter X marks the point on the Earth's surface from which the waves in Figure 2 are drawn. The point of the surface vertically above the place where the rocks break is the **epicentre**. The focus (hypocentre) is the point of origin of the earthquake inside the Earth, and the two words are synonyms, so they cannot be the single best answer for a point drawn on the surface. An isoseismic line joins places that suffered the same intensity of shaking; there is no such thing as an isoseismic point for the origin of the waves.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Why are P and S waves not received by seismographic stations located around Y? (use Figure 2, shown with question 5)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The zone Y is the **shadow zone**. When the waves reach the outer core (liquid), the P waves are strongly **refracted** (they slow down and bend), so they emerge beyond the shadow zone (about 103 to 142 degrees from the epicentre) and none arrives inside it. The S waves are shear waves and **cannot be transmitted through a liquid**, so they stop at the core-mantle boundary and are missing for all the stations on the far side. Option D is only half of the explanation: P waves do travel through a liquid, they are bent by it. A and B do not describe what happens at the core boundary.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: P and S waves are refracted deeper into the Earth's interior.
P and S waves are reflected back to the surface.
The P waves are refracted while the S waves are not transmitted.
P and S waves encounter a liquid medium.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal model below (Figure 3) and answer questions 7, 8 and 9.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

The symmetry elements of the crystal model above are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The model is a double pyramid (bipyramid) whose two horizontal axes X and Y are at right angles and equal, while the vertical axis Z has a different length: it belongs to the **tetragonal system**. Its symmetry elements are: **5 planes** (the horizontal plane and 4 vertical planes, 2 parallel to the crystal axes and 2 along the diagonals), **5 axes** (one four-fold axis along Z and four two-fold axes in the horizontal plane) and **a centre**. The set 9 planes, 13 axes, centre belongs to the cubic (isometric) system, and 3 planes, 3 axes, centre to the orthorhombic system.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What are the Miller indices of face A? (use Figure 3, shown with question 7)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Face A is the upper front-left face: it contains the front horizontal edge of the crystal and goes up to the top corner. The X axis leaves the crystal at the middle of that edge, so the face cuts the X axis at the unit distance, and it cuts the Z axis at the unit distance (the top corner). The edge is parallel to the Y axis, so the face is **parallel to Y** and cuts it at infinity. Intercepts $1,\ \infty,\ 1$ give the reciprocals $1,\ 0,\ 1$, so the Miller indices are **(101)**. A face cutting all three axes at the unit distance would be (111), and (011) would be parallel to X.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The letters X, Y and Z represent (use Figure 3, shown with question 7):
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 3 the lines X, Y and Z cross at the centre of the crystal and are the reference lines used to describe the faces of the crystal and to give them Miller indices. They are the **crystallographic axes** (the axes $a$, $b$ and $c$ of the crystal system). Axes of symmetry are a different notion: they are the lines about which the crystal can be rotated to repeat its appearance.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Give two diagnostic properties of quartz.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Quartz ($\mathrm{SiO_2}$) has a **hardness of 7** on Mohs' scale (it scratches glass and steel) and a **vitreous (glassy) lustre**. It has **no cleavage** and breaks with a conchoidal fracture. A is wrong because quartz has no cleavage, B is wrong because hardness 8 is that of topaz, and C gives a correct fracture but a wrong hardness (6 is that of orthoclase).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Olivine is a nesosilicate mineral with two end members. Name and give their formulae:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Olivine, $(\mathrm{Mg,Fe})_2\mathrm{SiO_4}$, is a solid solution series between the magnesium end member **forsterite**, $\mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4}$, and the iron end member **fayalite**, $\mathrm{Fe_2SiO_4}$. Enstatite ($\mathrm{MgSiO_3}$) is an orthopyroxene (a single chain silicate) and hornblende is an amphibole (a double chain silicate), so options B, C and D are wrong.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following mineral is an alumino-silicate?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The aluminosilicate minerals are the three polymorphs of $\mathrm{Al_2SiO_5}$: **andalusite**, kyanite and sillimanite, typical minerals of metamorphic rocks. Tourmaline is a complex boron silicate, olivine is a magnesium-iron silicate and garnet is a nesosilicate of the type $\mathrm{A_3B_2(SiO_4)_3}$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Very light vesicular volcanic rocks formed from acid magma are known as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Pumice** is a very light, pale, highly vesicular glassy rock formed when acid (silica-rich, viscous and gas-rich) magma froths as it erupts; it is so full of cavities that it can float on water. Scoria is a dark, vesicular rock from basic magma and is heavier. Bombs are large pieces of lava thrown out in flight, and tuffs are consolidated volcanic ash.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 4) illustrates an explosive volcanic eruption. Samples of pyroclastic debris collected at point A measure more than 64 mm and those at point B measure less than 64 mm in diameter. Use it to answer questions 14 and 15.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

What collective term is given to the pyroclastic debris collected at points A and B?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Tephra** is the collective name for all the fragmental material thrown into the air by an explosive eruption, whatever its size: blocks and bombs (more than 64 mm, point A) and lapilli and ash (less than 64 mm, point B). Ash and cinder are only the finer size classes, and a nuee ardente is a glowing cloud of gas and ash that flows down a slope, not a name for the debris collected.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Debris at locality B are found to have been welded by the residual heat of the eruption. Identify the rock most likely to have been formed: (use Figure 4, shown with question 14)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Fine pyroclastic debris (ash and lapilli) that is still hot when it settles sticks together (is welded) by its own residual heat and forms a hard rock called **ignimbrite** (a welded tuff, formed from pyroclastic flows). Volcanic breccia and agglomerate are made of coarse angular or rounded blocks and bombs that are not welded, and basalt is a lava, not a pyroclastic rock.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following drawings (Figure 5) show details of two igneous rocks. Study the diagram and answer questions 16 and 17.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

The textures shown by diagrams A and B respectively are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Diagram A shows a fine-grained groundmass (tiny particles of plagioclase, augite and olivine) with rounded cavities, some empty and some **filled with calcite**: the cavities are former gas bubbles, and cavities filled with a secondary mineral make the texture **amygdaloidal**. Diagram B shows a few large crystals of orthoclase set among smaller crystals of quartz, plagioclase and biotite: large crystals (phenocrysts) in a finer groundmass give a **porphyritic** texture. A purely vesicular texture would show only empty cavities, and graphic, pegmatitic, spherulitic and ophitic textures are not shown by these drawings.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the name given to the large orthoclase crystals in rock B? (use Figure 5, shown with question 16)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The large, well-formed crystals scattered in a finer groundmass of an igneous rock with a porphyritic texture are called **phenocrysts**. Porphyroblasts are large crystals that grow in a metamorphic rock, clasts are fragments of a sedimentary rock, and porphyrite is the name of a rock, not of a crystal.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An igneous rock X was analyzed as having the following chemical composition: $\mathrm{SiO_2} = 53\%$; $\mathrm{Al_2O_3} = 17.5\%$; $\mathrm{Na_2O} = 0.60\%$; $\mathrm{K_2O} = 5.3\%$; others $= 23.6\%$. If this rock has a fine grained texture, it is most likely:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The percentages add up to $53 + 17.5 + 0.60 + 5.3 + 23.6 = 100\%$. A silica content of 53 % places the rock in the **intermediate** class (about 52 to 66 % $\mathrm{SiO_2}$). The fine-grained (extrusive or shallow) intermediate rock is **andesite**. Rhyolite is acid (more than 66 % silica), basalt is basic (less than 52 % silica) and dolerite is a basic rock of medium grain size.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following features indicates subsidence of the sea floor?

*Options as printed:* A) Sea arches   B) Coastal waterfalls   C) Raised beaches   D) Wave cut platforms
questions.corrige_markdown:
When the sea floor subsides the ocean basins become deeper and the sea level falls relative to the land: the coast **emerges**. Old beaches are then left stranded above the present high tide level, as **raised beaches**, which is the classic evidence of a fall of the sea level. Sea arches and wave cut platforms are formed by marine erosion at the present sea level (they show emergence only if found raised), and coastal waterfalls (hanging valleys) can also be linked to a fall of the sea level. Several options can therefore be argued, which is why the question is left open.

**Intended answer: C (Raised beaches).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Pebbles faceted by the abrasive effects of wind-blown sand are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Pebbles and rocks in a desert that are sandblasted by wind-driven sand grains are worn into flat, polished faces (facets) with sharp edges: they are called **ventifacts** (dreikanter when they have three facets). Millet seed grains are rounded, frosted sand grains, a desert pavement is a surface of pebbles left after the wind has removed the fine material, and a rock pedestal is a rock narrowed at its base by abrasion.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Streams consisting of interwoven channels are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **braided stream** is made of many shallow channels that divide and rejoin around bars of sand and gravel; it forms where the river carries more load than it can transport (steep slope, variable discharge, easily eroded banks). A graded stream is in equilibrium between erosion and deposition, a consequent stream flows down the original slope of the land, and a subsequent stream follows a belt of weak rock along the strike.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following sedimentary rock types is formed by rapid deposition in a deep marine environment?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Greywackes** are poorly sorted, dark sandstones with a clay-rich matrix that are deposited quickly by turbidity currents on the continental slope and in deep marine basins (turbidites, with graded bedding). Black shale forms slowly from fine mud in quiet, oxygen-poor water, arkose is a feldspar-rich sandstone deposited near a granite source by rivers or alluvial fans, and a lithic sandstone is a sandstone rich in rock fragments of various origins.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the information given below and answer questions 23 and 24. Sediments were collected from an environment. After sieving, it was discovered that the sediments were of markedly different grain sizes.

Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from the sediments? The sediments are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Sorting describes how uniform the grain size is. Sediments in which sieving separates grains of **markedly different sizes** are **poorly sorted**. Sediments carried far from their source are generally better sorted and better rounded, graded bedding is a structure of a bed (one cannot see it in a loose sample) and a moderately sorted sediment would show a limited range of sizes.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The possible environment where the sediments might have been collected is: (use the information given before question 23)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Poorly sorted sediments, with grains ranging from clay and silt to sand and boulders, are typical of **glacial deposits (till or boulder clay)**, because ice transports and drops all sizes together without sorting. Wind in deserts, waves in shallow seas and on beaches all sort the grains well, giving uniform sands.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which textural term is applied to metamorphic rocks consisting of equidimensional mineral grains?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **granoblastic** texture is a mosaic of interlocking grains of about the same size in all directions (equidimensional or equant grains), as in marble and quartzite. Idioblastic describes crystals with their own well-formed faces, hornfelsic is the fine-grained texture of contact-metamorphosed rocks (hornfels), and decussate describes a random criss-cross arrangement of elongate crystals.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a low grade metamorphic rock?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Green schist is formed under low temperature (about 300 to 500 $^\circ$C) and low to moderate pressure, in the greenschist facies (chlorite, actinolite, albite and epidote): it is a **low grade** rock. Amphibolite and garnet mica schist are medium to high grade, and blue schist forms at high pressure and low temperature, in subduction zones, so it belongs to a different facies series.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the temperature and pressure condition under which sanidinite facies are formed?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **sanidinite facies** is the facies of the highest temperature and the lowest pressure of contact metamorphism: it is found in the contact zone of a hot intrusion or lava (xenoliths baked in basalt, for example), where sanidine and other high temperature minerals form. High temperature with high pressure gives the granulite and eclogite facies, low temperature with high pressure gives the blueschist facies.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following features is produced as a result of the collision between an Oceanic Plate and a Continental Plate?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Andes** formed where the dense oceanic Nazca Plate is subducted beneath the continental South American Plate; subduction causes the folding, volcanism and uplift of the mountain chain. The Himalayas and the Alps are the result of the collision of two continental plates, and the Mid-Atlantic ridge is a divergent (constructive) plate boundary.

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following rock types is most likely to be found along a transform plate boundary?
questions.corrige_markdown:
At a transform boundary two plates slide past each other along a fault, and the shearing grinds and recrystallises the rocks along the fault zone into a **mylonite** (a fault rock formed by ductile shear). Rhyolite, andesite and dacite are volcanic rocks of divergent and especially convergent (subduction) margins; there is little or no volcanism at a transform boundary.

**Answer: C.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: A transform fault is an example of a/an:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a transform fault the blocks move **horizontally** past each other, parallel to the strike of the fault plane: this is a **strike-slip fault** (the San Andreas fault is an example). In a dip-slip fault the movement is up or down the dip, and a normal fault is a dip-slip fault caused by tension. An oblique-slip fault has both components.

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 6) which shows folded beds, and answer questions 31 and 32.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

If the fold is an anticline, what is the order of deposition of the beds?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Figure 6 the beds are arranged symmetrically, d c b a b c d, with bed a in the middle. In an **anticline** the oldest beds are in the core and the beds get younger away from the axis. Bed a is therefore the oldest, followed by b, then c, then d, which is the youngest. The order of deposition (oldest first) is **a, b, c, d**. The order d, c, b, a would be correct for a syncline.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: d, c, a, b, c, d

questions.enonce_markdown:
The fold shown by the diagram is a/an: (use Figure 6, shown with question 31)

*Options as printed:* A) Asymmetrical syncline   B) Symmetrical anticline   C) Asymmetrical anticline   D) Symmetrical syncline
questions.corrige_markdown:
The beds repeat in the same way on both sides of the middle bed a (d c b a b c d) and the pattern is mirrored about a vertical line, so the fold is **symmetrical** (the two limbs have the same dip and the axial plane is vertical), which excludes the asymmetrical options. Whether it is an anticline or a syncline depends on the ages of the beds, which the figure does not print: with bed a the oldest, as assumed in question 31, it is an anticline, and with bed a the youngest it would be a syncline. The question is therefore left open.

**Intended answer: B (Symmetrical anticline).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following groups of organisms shows a planktonic mode of life?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Planktonic organisms drift passively in the surface water. The **graptoloids** (graptolites) were colonial animals that floated in the water column, which is why they are widespread and good zone fossils of the Lower Palaeozoic. Ammonoids and nautiloids were free-swimming (nektonic) cephalopods and brachiopods lived fixed on the sea floor (benthic).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the fossil diagram (Figure 7) which shows the internal morphology of a valve and answer questions 34 and 35.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

Identify the structures labelled O and P respectively:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Figure 7 is the inside of a brachiopod valve. The structure O is the opening at the beak (umbo), the **delthyrium**, the triangular or circular opening through which the pedicle passed. The two elongate scars towards the middle of the valve, to which P points, are the attachment areas of the **diductor muscles** (the muscles that open the shell). A brachidium (the supporting loop of the lophophore) and sockets belong to the other (brachial) valve, so options A and D do not fit a valve with a delthyrium, and the structure O is not a tooth.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The valve shown in the diagram above is the: (use Figure 7, shown with question 34)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A valve that has a **delthyrium** (the opening for the pedicle at the beak) and diductor muscle scars is the **pedicle (ventral) valve**, the larger valve of a brachiopod. The brachial (dorsal) valve carries the sockets, the cardinal process and the brachidium. The words right and left valve are used for bivalve molluscs, not for brachiopods, which have a ventral and a dorsal valve.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is a period of the Lower Paleozoic?

*Options as printed:* A) Permian   B) Triassic   C) Devonian   D) Carboniferous
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the usual division the Lower Palaeozoic is made of the Cambrian, the Ordovician and the Silurian: none of the four periods printed belongs to it. The Permian and the Carboniferous are Upper Palaeozoic, the Triassic is the first period of the Mesozoic. The Devonian, which follows the Silurian directly, is the oldest of the four options, and is the one the setter most probably means; strictly it belongs to the Middle and Upper Palaeozoic, which is why the question is left open.

**Intended answer: C (Devonian).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following time divisions covers almost three quarters of all geologic time?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Precambrian** (Hadean, Archaean and Proterozoic) lasts from the formation of the Earth, about 4.6 billion years ago, to the start of the Cambrian, 541 million years ago: about $4.06$ billion years out of $4.6$, which is about 88 % of geological time (the "almost three quarters" of the question is an approximation). The Phanerozoic is only about 12 %, the Proterozoic alone about 43 % and the Cambrian about 56 million years. The Precambrian is the only division that covers a large majority of the time scale.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: "In an undisturbed series of sedimentary rocks the oldest rocks are at the bottom and progressively younger rocks are found towards the top". This is the Principle of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
This is the **Principle of Superposition** (Steno): in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary beds, each bed is younger than the one below it. Uniformitarianism states that present processes explain the past, faunal succession says that fossils succeed each other in a definite order, and the cross-cutting principle says that a feature that cuts across a rock is younger than that rock.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two examples of humic coal include:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Humic coals form from woody plant debris, and the rank series is peat, **lignite**, sub-bituminous, **bituminous** coal and anthracite. Boghead (algal) and cannel (spores) coals are sapropelic coals, formed from algae, spores and finely divided plant debris in stagnant water, so any option that includes them is wrong.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Silver and gold mineralization have been found in veins around a granitic intrusion. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hot, mineral-rich water driven out of the cooling granite circulates in the fractures of the country rock, cools, and deposits quartz, gold and silver in **veins**: this is **hydrothermal activity**. Magmatic segregation concentrates minerals (chromite, for instance) within the magma itself, pneumatolysis involves hot gases at higher temperatures, forming tin and tungsten deposits, and supergene enrichment is a near-surface weathering process that enriches an existing deposit.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A major iron ore deposit in Cameroon is located at:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The major iron ore deposit of Cameroon is the **Mbalam** deposit (Mbalam-Nabeba, in the East Region, on the Congo craton). Ngaoundal and Minim-Martap are known for bauxite (the ore of aluminium) and Betare Oya for alluvial and vein gold.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Slate is a material often used for roofing because it:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Slate is a low grade metamorphic rock with a well-developed **slaty cleavage**, formed when clay minerals (mica, chlorite) are aligned perpendicular to the pressure. The rock therefore splits easily into thin, flat, lightweight and durable sheets that make good roofing tiles. Impermeability is a useful property but is not the reason why slate is used instead of other rocks; fine grain and bedding are not what makes it split.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A formation that contains sufficient saturated permeable material to yield significant quantities of water to wells and springs is called an:
questions.corrige_markdown:
An **aquifer** is a saturated, permeable and porous rock layer (sandstone, gravel, fractured limestone) that stores water and yields it in useful quantities to wells and springs. An aquitard transmits water only very slowly, an aquiclude is saturated but does not transmit usable amounts (clay), and an aquifuge neither contains nor transmits water (solid granite).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a secondary volcanic hazard?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Primary hazards are the direct products of the eruption: ash fall, lava flows, gases and pyroclastic flows (nuee ardentes). Secondary hazards happen afterwards, as a consequence of the eruption: **lahars** (mudflows formed when volcanic ash is mobilised by rain or by melting snow and ice), floods and landslides. Soil liquefaction is a hazard of earthquakes.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following is most likely to cause flooding?

*Options as printed:* A) Deforestation   B) Thunder and tropical storms   C) Building around stream banks   D) Building construction
questions.corrige_markdown:
A flood happens when the water supplied to a river (or to the land) exceeds the capacity of the channel. The direct cause of this excess water is **heavy rain, such as thunderstorms and tropical storms**. Deforestation, building on stream banks and construction (paved surfaces) make the floods worse by increasing the runoff and reducing the capacity of the channel, but they are aggravating factors rather than the trigger. As several options can be defended, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (Thunder and tropical storms).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following rocks is the oldest in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The oldest rocks of Cameroon belong to the Precambrian basement (the Congo craton and the Pan-African belt), which is made of metamorphic rocks such as **gneiss** and of granites. The basalts of Bakingili belong to the young volcanic Cameroon Line (Cenozoic), and the shales and sandstones are sedimentary rocks of the Cretaceous to Tertiary sedimentary basins that rest on the basement, so they are much younger than the gneiss.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is a coastal basin in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Rio del Rey Basin** lies on the Atlantic coast of Cameroon, in the south-west, at the head of the Gulf of Guinea (with the Douala-Kribi/Campo basin it is one of the coastal sedimentary basins, with oil). The Mamfe, Yola-Garoua (Benue trough) and Djerem-Mbere basins are interior (continental) basins.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What distance on the land is represented by a length of 5 cm on a map of scale 1/50000?
questions.corrige_markdown:
At the scale 1/50 000, 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm on the ground. For 5 cm: $5 \times 50\,000 = 250\,000\ \mathrm{cm}$. Converting to metres (divide by 100): $250\,000 \div 100 = 2\,500\ \mathrm{m}$, which is 2.5 km. The other options come from errors of a power of ten in the conversion.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 8) and answer questions 49 and 50.

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2021-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

The lines labelled X, Y and Z are called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The straight, parallel and equally spaced lines X, Y and Z join the points where the boundary of a bed (the solid line) crosses topographic contours of the same height: they are the lines of equal height on the surface of the bed, called **stratum contours** (structure contours), and they give the strike of the bed. Their regular spacing shows a constant dip. The bed boundary is the solid line, a bedding plane is the surface itself and the contour numbers are the heights written on the contours.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Lines X, Y and Z represent equal heights above sea level. Which height is represented by line Y? (use Figure 8, shown with question 49)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The topographic contours of Figure 8 are labelled 200, 300 and 400 m. The line Z meets the bed boundary exactly where the 400 m contour does, so Z is the 400 m stratum contour. The three lines are parallel and equally spaced, and the contour interval is 100 m, so the heights of the stratum contours are 400 m (Z), **300 m (Y)** and 200 m (X). The height of Y is therefore 300 m.

**Answer: D.**
